spans.claim: The auctioneer announced Lot 191 as imperfect and sold it
spans.anchor: Lot 191 is imperfect and is sold not subject to return
spans.span: Lot 191 is imperfect and is sold not subject to return; a very desirable volume all the same.

spans.claim: The delivery note was mistakenly filled as Lot 191 instead of Lot 91
spans.anchor: sale clerk, in the stress of his duties, inadvertently filled in the delivery note as Lot 191
spans.span: My sale clerk, in the stress of his duties, inadvertently filled in the delivery note as Lot 191.

spans.claim: Mr Powis received back the Virginiola book with formal regrets
spans.anchor: the book was returned to me this morning

spans.claim: Mr Chatton wrote to dealers pretending to buy a copy for collation
spans.anchor: I wrote to a few dealers, rather, I am afraid, giving them the impression that we wished to buy a copy
spans.span: So I wrote to a few dealers, rather, I am afraid, giving them the impression that we wished to buy a copy.

spans.claim: Mr Chatton secretly sold the original Virginiola before the auction
spans.anchor: he had already sold the Virginiola himself only a week before

spans.claim: The stolen book was disguised by removing and replacing pages
spans.anchor: the abstracted sheet was cunningly replaced, probably certain erasable marks that had been put in for fuller disguise were removed
spans.span: The _Virginiola_ was recovered; the abstracted sheet was cunningly replaced, probably certain erasable marks that had been put in for fuller disguise were removed, and Mr Powis received back his property with formal regrets.

spans.claim: Mr Powis did not have a receipt for the book because it was paid by cheque initialed to bearer
spans.anchor: I was making out a cheque when he reminded me that his right hand was useless and asked me to initial it to ‘bearer.’ That is why I come to have no receipt
spans.span: I was making out a cheque when he reminded me that his right hand was useless and asked me to initial it to 'bearer.' That is why I come to have no receipt.

spans.claim: The purchaser took away the wrong lot due to delivery note error
spans.anchor: Another purchaser bought certain lots. Among them was Lot 91. My sale clerk... inadvertently filled in the delivery note as Lot 191

spans.claim: Mr Chatton’s motive was financial need and deception
spans.anchor: he had expenses. Perhaps he had fallen into the hands of the Jews; perhaps it was the Jewesses

spans.claim: The auction house was slow to turn the case over to the police
spans.anchor: you will find more profit in investigating farther afield
spans.span: Unless one of your people happens to come forward with a real clue, Mr Ing, I venture to predict that you will find more profit in investigating farther afield.

spans.claim: Mr Marrable was interested in the Virginiola and its market value
spans.anchor: I should certainly like to land the Virginiola

spans.claim: The stolen book was sold as imperfect to reduce suspicion
spans.anchor: if at the sale it was discovered to be imperfect in an important detail then it might realise only a fraction of that sum
spans.span: Now the _Virginiola_ had been valued at £300 by old Sir Vernon, but if at the sale it was discovered to be imperfect in an important detail then it might realise only a fraction of that sum.

spans.claim: Mr Powis was worried about rumors affecting his business
spans.anchor: My name has been connected with a stolen copy and buyers are very shy

spans.claim: Mr Chatton’s scheme involved buying back the book before the sale
spans.anchor: The first thing was to get back the Virginiola a little before the sale

spans.claim: Mr Chatton’s plan failed because the market value had risen
spans.anchor: What he had not taken into account was the enormous rise in the value of this class of work
spans.span: What he had not taken into account was the enormous rise in the value of this class of work.

spans.claim: The secretary’s scheme was speculative and left no evidence
spans.anchor: Chatton... did not leave behind him one solitary shred of evidence that would stand before a jury

spans.claim: Mr Carrados advised the auction house to verify the stolen book’s status
spans.anchor: I would suggest that we eliminate Mr Dillworthy... What remains?

spans.claim: The purchaser’s buying pattern was suspicious but not conclusive
spans.anchor: Mr Dillworthy bought 91 at a good price. After that he did nothing until 191 had passed. Then he secured four lots of cheap books

spans.claim: The purchaser declined to write his name on the back of a banknote
spans.anchor: He held out a bank-note... I gave him a pen... He handed me the pen back and said: ‘Thanks; after all, I’ll leave it as it is.’
